findings.trigger_condition: When two equal nodes exist where one is hashable and the other is unhashable (__hash__ = None), and both appear in the edge stream
findings.root_cause: The hashable lookup path (hash_buckets) and unhashable lookup path (unhashable_nodes list) are completely separate silos. The unhashable path only scans unhashable_nodes (line 44), and the hashable path only scans the hash bucket (line 53). When node H (hashable) equals node U (unhashable), they are assigned different IDs because neither lookup path checks the other's storage.
findings.impact: Equal nodes are incorrectly treated as distinct nodes. This breaks the topological sort correctness: edges that should apply to a single logical node get split across two separate nodes, potentially causing wrong layer assignments, missed dependency ordering, or false cycle detections. The algorithm violates the contract that equal node values should be deduplicated.
findings.suggested_validation: Create a hashable class and an unhashable class that compare equal to each other. Pass edges involving both: [(hashable_instance, 'dep1'), (unhashable_instance, 'dep2')]. The result should show one layer-1 node, but it currently shows two separate nodes.

findings.trigger_condition: When there are many unhashable nodes in the input (typically hundreds or more)
findings.root_cause: The unhashable lookup path performs a linear scan through unhashable_ids/unhashable_nodes for every new node. For N unhashable nodes, this creates O(N²) time complexity since every lookup scans all previously-seen unhashable nodes.
findings.impact: Performance degrades quadratically with the number of unhashable nodes. With 800 unhashable nodes, the lookup alone takes ~30ms, and this grows rapidly with larger inputs. This violates the implicit performance contract for topological sort algorithms which should be linear in the number of edges and nodes.
findings.suggested_validation: Benchmark with 100, 200, 400, 800 unhashable nodes (e.g., lists). Measure runtime: the O(N²) factor (time/N²) will be roughly constant, confirming quadratic growth.

findings.trigger_condition: When many hashable nodes share the same hash value (hash collisions), either intentionally or due to poor hash functions
findings.root_cause: When a hash collision occurs, the code performs a linear scan through the entire collision bucket (lines 53-56) checking equality against every existing node in that bucket. When many nodes share the same hash, this becomes O(N) per lookup, causing O(N²) overall time complexity.
findings.impact: Performance degrades quadratically when inputs have many nodes with colliding hashes. A malicious or pathological input could intentionally create hash collisions to cause a denial of service. With 800 nodes all sharing hash=0, the runtime is ~40ms and grows quadratically.
findings.suggested_validation: Create a class with __hash__ always returning 0. Benchmark with 100, 200, 400, 800 nodes. The O(N²) factor (time/N²) will be roughly constant (~0.06-0.08 microseconds), confirming quadratic behavior.
